Mawkish

/MAW-kish/ - the stress falls on MAW · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Mawkish means characterized by sick sentimentality.

The gift-shop poems struck her as mawkish, all angel wings and rhyming sunsets with no real feeling underneath.

Worked Example

The catalog copy for the memorial bench was mawkish overreach — 'where angels rest and grandpas watch forever' — and the carpenter refused to print it, saying the oak could speak for itself.

Mawkish is the harshest word on the sentimentality shelf: emotion so exaggerated and false that it sickens instead of moving. The history is literal — the word began as 'maggoty,' sickening like spoiled meat — and the stomach-turn survives in its meaning.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

syrupy: sticky-sweet in tone, laid on thick

treacly: drowning in sugary feeling — the British flavor of the same fault

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

understated: lets the feeling speak in a whisper

unsentimental: refuses emotional decoration altogether

Where it sits · how sickly and false the tenderness turns — sweet → syrupy → mawkish

sweet vs. mawkish: Sweet is far milder than mawkish — genuine tenderness that nobody could object to.

syrupy vs. mawkish: Syrupy is weaker than mawkish — heavily sweet, but not yet the false, sickening sentiment that makes an audience cringe.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — mawk

Root — mawk: maggot (Middle English mawke)

Suffix — -ish

Suffix — -ish: having the quality of

Put it together

Put it together: Mawk (maggot) + -ish (having the quality of) = maggoty. Mawkish first described food gone bad — sickening, like spoiled meat — and then slid from the stomach to the heart: sentiment so overdone and so false that it produces the same queasy turn. The maggot rotted away; the nausea stayed.

The maggot inside the word

The maggot inside the word: Middle English mawke, 'maggot,' survives nowhere else in the modern language, so mawkish has no living relatives to spot. What it kept instead is the feeling: when critics call an ending mawkish, they are literally saying it turned their stomach.

Strength Check

Word Choice

critical

Mawkish is the strongest insult in the sentimentality family: emotion so false and sugary it sickens — remember the maggot in its history. Use sentimental for mild cases, and its unit-mate maudlin for tearful, self-indulgent people; save mawkish for art and rhetoric — the ad, the ending, the verse — that begs for tears it never earned.
